name: Olga Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at the big open-pit iron ore mine outside town, twelve-hour shifts, four on and four off. I take the empty truck down the ramp to the shovel, wait to be loaded, then crawl back up to the crusher with about 220 tonnes on the back. I've been doing it two years and I'm still the slowest at spotting under the shovel, which the shovel operator, Vic, likes to remind me about over the radio. What I love is the dawn on the night shift, when the whole pit goes pink and you're alone up there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the money side of your life look like right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, good. The pay is high for someone with only a school certificate, and I've got about ten months of wages put away. Tomas, my partner, drives buses for the city, and we bought a small flat together last year with a big deposit, so the mortgage is low. There are three other mines within an hour's drive, so if this one closed I wouldn't be on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, that's the boring one. If AI stays hype, my truck stays my truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly to the guys on my crew who keep forwarding videos of trucks with no cabs. At the union meeting I'd say it's a good reminder that the company sells every new gadget as a revolution. Online I wouldn't say anything, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I'm doing and I get better at it. The real worries are the old ones: iron ore prices, the company cutting a shift when the price drops, my back after ten years of bouncing in a cab. I'd still worry about the iron ore price more than any robot, because that's what cut the night shift at my mine in 2024.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving, keep putting a third of every pay into savings, and do the loader ticket the company keeps offering, because a second machine makes you harder to cut. Next year I'd like to pay an extra chunk off the flat. That's it, nothing fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Steady is what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said prices worry you. What happened when the night shift was cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They moved forty of us onto days and dropped the night allowance, which was about a sixth of my pay. Nobody lost their job, but people with kids really felt it. Me and Tomas just stopped eating out for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any small thing AI might still change in your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the dispatch system, the screen in the cab that tells you which shovel to go to. If that gets a bit smarter, fine, I'll still just follow the arrow. I don't touch any of that stuff unless I have to.

say: I'd tell my crew the **robot hype** was always the company selling gadgets.
I'd remind people at the union meeting that **prices**, not AI, decide our shifts.
think: My **truck job** stays mine, and I keep getting better at spotting under the shovel.
My real worries stay the old ones: **ore prices**, shift cuts and my back.
do: Keep putting a **third of each pay** into savings.
Take the **loader ticket** the company offers, so a second machine protects her.
Pay an **extra chunk** off the flat next year.
feel: **Relieved**, because steady is exactly what she wants.
S0.quote: I'd still worry about the iron ore price more than any robot, because that's what cut the night shift at my mine in 2024.
fieldNote: Her **savings and low mortgage** make the plateau feel secure, not just familiar.
She ties risk to the **2024 night-shift cut**, not to technology.
She avoids the cab **dispatch screen** beyond the minimum, a sign of how resistant she is.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck on the same four-on, four-off roster
Put a third of every pay into the savings account
Pay an extra lump off the shared flat mortgage next year
Sit the loader ticket the company already offers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's more real. Robots coming slowly is still robots coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the union has to get in the room now, before the first driverless trucks turn up, not after. I'd say it plainly at the next meeting: no driverless fleet without a deal on jobs. To friends I'd say the office people should be more scared than us for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the junior driver, and I'm the slowest. If they bring in a few driverless trucks, they don't sack the guy with fifteen years, they sack me. The company would keep Vic (the shovel operator) and the old drivers, and the first truck job to go would be mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and sign up as a delegate for our crew, which I've been avoiding. I'd get the loader ticket and the dozer ticket in the first year, because the machines that work in mud and tight corners will be the last to go driverless. And I'd stop spending on anything big, no new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest. I don't like change, and I really don't like change I can't argue with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says AI takes thinking tasks first. Where does that touch your mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planners and the dispatch office, the people who decide where the trucks go. If software does the planning, maybe fewer of them, and the ones left push us harder on cycle times. So it reaches me through the screen in the cab before it reaches me through a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go to one of the other mines nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to. The other three are all owned by big companies too, and they'd all be buying the same trucks. Moving wouldn't fix anything, it'd just make me the new junior again.

say: I'd push the **union** to get a jobs deal before **driverless trucks** arrive.
I'd tell friends the **office jobs** feel this first, before miners do.
think: As the **junior and slowest driver**, she expects to be cut first.
Software planning means **tighter cycle-time targets** through her cab screen before any robot comes.
do: Sign up as **union delegate** for her crew at the next meeting.
Get the **loader and dozer tickets** within the first year.
Put off any **big purchase**, starting with the new car.
feel: **Tight in her chest**, because she dislikes change she can't argue with.
S1.quote: The company would keep Vic (the shovel operator) and the old drivers, and the first truck job to go would be mine.
fieldNote: She is **clear-eyed** that seniority, not skill alone, decides who goes.
Her answer to change is **collective**: get in the room as a union.
She won't move mines because **every owner** would buy the same trucks.

steps.text: Sign up as union delegate for her crew at the next meeting
Get the loader and dozer tickets in the first year
Put off buying a new car and other big costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I'd even be a proper driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it loud: this is exactly why we need a government that steps in, with rules on how fast mines can drop people and real money for the ones they drop. I'd say it at the union, and I'd even go to a rally, which I've never done. I'd tell my mum not to panic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking part goes in 2028, so dispatch and planning are gone, and the trucks already almost drive themselves on some mines. Then real robots by 2031. Driving a haul truck is the easiest job in a mine to hand to a robot, and I'm the junior driver who'd be out first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop all spending that isn't the mortgage and food, and push savings from ten months towards a year and a half. I'd join the rally and the union fight for a payout deal. In the year after, I'd look at what the robots can't do yet, maybe the workshop, but honestly I'd be learning that from scratch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. I'd be lying awake next to Tomas doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're fine for a while because of the flat and the savings, and that I'm scared anyway. Buses will go driverless too, so it's not like one of us is the safe one. I'd probably cry, then make a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the workshop. Is that something you'd really do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it, but yes, if it was that or nothing. The difference between the 2028 picture and the slower ones is I don't get to wait and see what works. I'd have to jump into something I don't know while I'm scared.

say: I'd demand **government rules** on how fast mines can cut people.
I'd go to my **first rally** and fight for a real payout deal.
think: Haul driving is the **easiest mine job** to automate, and she is the junior.
Dispatch goes in **2028**, robot trucks by **2031**, so she has roughly five years.
do: Cut all spending except **mortgage and food** straight away.
Push savings from ten months toward **eighteen months** of wages.
Start learning **workshop skills** in the year after, though it means starting from scratch.
feel: **Sick**, lying awake doing sums next to Tomas.
**Scared** even though the flat and savings give them time.
S2.quote: Driving a haul truck is the easiest job in a mine to hand to a robot, and I'm the junior driver who'd be out first.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job**, and her partner's bus job is exposed too.
The **short warning** removes her habit of waiting to see what works.
Her first instinct is **politics and protest**, then savings, then reluctant retraining.

steps.text: Cut spending to the mortgage, food and bills only
Build savings from ten months up to eighteen months of wages
March in her first rally for limits on mine layoffs
Start learning workshop skills once robot trucks are announced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking part, eight for the robots. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things, but with a plan attached: the union should be bargaining now for retraining money and a slow handover. I'd vote for whoever promised to tax the robot fleets and put it back into the mining towns. I'd say it at the pub too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, eight years until the robots means I'd be 35 when the truck goes. That's young enough to start again, but I'd have wasted my twenties on a job that disappears. By 2034 I'd be 35, still the junior on my crew, and holding a ticket for a truck that drives itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years getting every ticket the company pays for, and I'd put my name down for the maintenance apprenticeship even though I'm not mechanical. I'd keep saving hard and pay the flat down so it's nearly gone by 2034. And I'd work on the union campaign every month, not just when it's on fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but not panicked. More like dread with a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rina on my crew, she's 52 and only knows trucks. She'd be too young to retire and too old for an apprenticeship. People like her are why I'd fight for the payout deal, not just for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid new things. Would you really do the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down and then probably drag my feet. That's the honest answer. With five years' warning I can tell myself there's time, and that's the trap.

say: I'd want the **union bargaining now** for retraining money and a slow handover.
I'd vote for whoever **taxes robot fleets** and puts money back into mining towns.
think: She'd be **35** when the robot trucks arrive, holding a ticket for nothing.
Five years' warning tempts her to **drag her feet**, and she knows it.
do: Collect every **company-paid ticket** in the first two years.
Put her name down for the **maintenance apprenticeship** despite not being mechanical.
Pay the flat down so it's **nearly gone by 2034**.
feel: **Heavy dread**, but with a calendar rather than panic.
S3.quote: By 2034 I'd be 35, still the junior on my crew, and holding a ticket for a truck that drives itself.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose the truck job**; more time changes the plan, not the outcome.
She **admits** she'd probably stall on the apprenticeship.
Her concern for **Rina**, an older colleague, drives her union work.

steps.text: Collect every ticket the mine pays for in the next two years
Apply for the mine's maintenance apprenticeship
Pay off most of the flat mortgage before 2034
Work on the union's robot-fleet campaign every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. By then I'm 37 and maybe not even driving trucks anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse. Governments, companies and the union have ten years, and if miners still get thrown out with nothing, that's a choice. I'd keep saying that at meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's time to move to something steadier before it's forced on me. Robots in 2039 means a full career-change window. Ten years of warning means I'd be stupid to still be in a haul truck cab when the robots come. I'd just have to actually do it, which is the hard bit for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first few years I'd do the loader and dozer tickets, then ask for a move to the tyre bay or the workshop where I can learn on the job. I'd keep saving the same third. Tomas and I would talk about whether to stay near the mines or move closer to his family where there's more mixed work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It feels like something I could actually prepare for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you see yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ideally in the workshop or doing something like mine safety inspections. Something that needs a person to look at it and sign it off. I don't really know which of those would last, and that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you put it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being comfortable. The money's good, the flat's nearly paid, and every year it'd feel like next year is fine. I know myself.

say: With ten years, nobody has an **excuse** for throwing miners out.
I'd keep pushing the **union and government** to plan properly.
think: Ten years is a **full career-change window** if she actually uses it.
Her **comfort** with good pay is the main risk of stalling.
do: Finish the **loader and dozer tickets** in the first few years.
Ask for a move to the **tyre bay or workshop** to learn on the job.
Talk with Tomas about **moving nearer his family**, where work is more mixed.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to breathe, because she can prepare.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning means I'd be stupid to still be in a haul truck cab when the robots come.
fieldNote: She still sees her **truck job ending** but feels some control.
She **doesn't know** which hands-on roles would last, and that bothers her.
A possible **move** with Tomas appears only in this slower picture.

steps.text: Finish the loader and dozer tickets in the first few years
Ask to transfer to the tyre bay or workshop
Talk with Tomas about moving nearer his family
Keep raising robot-fleet planning at union meetings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily, because I'm the kind of person who needs time and that one gives me none. What would help is the union having a deal already signed: retraining on full pay and a proper payout for anyone who goes. Without a deal signed before the robots come, a junior truck driver like me is just a number on a spreadsheet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. Everyone asks about my job, but Tomas drives buses, and if both our jobs are in the same picture, our savings don't stretch as far as it looks.

headlineQuote: Without a deal signed before the robots come, a junior truck driver like me is just a number on a spreadsheet.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old** haul truck driver at an open-pit iron ore mine, two years in.
She has **ten months saved** and a low mortgage on a flat shared with Tomas, a bus driver.
She dislikes new technology and **never uses AI**, and admits she drags her feet on change.
Her answer to every scenario is **the union**: get a jobs deal signed before robots arrive.
She moves from **calm** in the plateau to **alarmed** in the fast AGI picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it gives her no time and she needs time to change.
whatWouldHelp: A **signed union deal** with retraining on full pay and a proper payout for anyone cut.
